reg.title: Natural Justice - The foundation of inquiries under POSH Act
reg.impact: POSH Act committees must operationally embed: (1) written notice of allegations with sufficient particularity; (2) reasonable opportunity for the accused to cross-examine witnesses and tender evidence; (3) absence of bias or predetermined outcome; (4) reasoned findings recorded. Non-compliance creates grounds for civil writ or industrial adjudication challenging dismissal or suspension.
reg.action: Draft POSH investigation SOPs explicitly documenting notice, hearing stages, witness examination rights, and recusal triggers; train internal committees on audi alteram partem compliance; maintain contemporaneous records of all procedural steps; consider independent external inquiry officer for senior respondents to shield against natural justice challenges.

sources.name: Bar & Bench
sources.blurb: Natural justice principles (audi alteram partem and nemo judex) are foundational to POSH Act inquiry procedures and their breach renders investigation findings legally vulnerable to challenge.

reg.title: When debtors hold on to the wheel: A comparative perspective on India's CIIRP and Singapore's Scheme of Arrangement
reg.impact: Practitioners advising distressed debtors must account for CIIRP's stricter insolvency triggers, mandatory court supervision, and inability to cherry-pick creditor classes-unlike Singapore schemes which permit moratoria and selective restructuring without formal insolvency admission.
reg.action: Transactional counsel structuring debtor-led workouts should evaluate whether CIIRP's Section 54 entry criteria are met early; consider whether pre-CIIRP creditor agreements can replicate scheme-like flexibility; and assess cross-border implications if the debtor has Singapore exposure.

sources.name: Bar & Bench
sources.blurb: CIIRP under India's IBC allows debtor-in-possession restructuring but lacks Singapore's flexible scheme framework, creating a narrower window for distressed companies to retain control while negotiating with creditors.

reg.title: When the Arbitration Clock runs out: A guide to Section 29A of the Arbitration Act
reg.impact: Parties lose arbitral remedy if award not rendered within 12 months; arbitrator loses power to decide the dispute; proceedings must cease unless extended by written agreement before expiry; any award rendered post-deadline is void or unenforceable.
reg.action: In retainer letters, arbitration clauses and appointment orders: (1) confirm commencement date precisely; (2) secure written extension agreements well before month 11; (3) track procedural calendar against 12-month clock; (4) brief clients on termination risk and cost of re-arbitration; (5) propose realistic timelines in Terms of Reference; (6) document all extensions in writing.

sources.name: Bar & Bench
sources.blurb: Section 29A imposes strict procedural termination of arbitral proceedings after 12 months unless extended, creating significant practical risk of loss of jurisdiction and finality if deadlines are breached.

reg.title: Surveillance without statute: The constitutional void in India's facial recognition policy
reg.impact: Facial recognition surveillance systems currently operate without statutory safeguards on collection, storage, use, or access-exposing users to unregulated identification and tracking in violation of privacy rights under Article 21.
reg.action: Parliament should enact a dedicated statute governing facial recognition use by state and private actors, specifying permissible purposes, data protection standards, consent/notification protocols, and judicial oversight-aligned with constitutional privacy principles post-*Puttaswamy*.

sources.name: Bar & Bench
sources.blurb: Article argues that facial recognition deployment in India lacks statutory underpinning and violates constitutional privacy norms-highlighting a governance gap requiring legislative action, not merely policy guidelines.

reg.title: Arbitrating a class action?
reg.impact: Corporates cannot use arbitration clauses to consolidate multiple consumer claims into a single arbitral proceeding without explicit legislative reform; each claimant needs independent consent.
reg.action: In structuring dispute resolution clauses for multi-party consumer or employment disputes, assume individual arbitration only; do not rely on class arbitration as a consolidation mechanism unless explicit statutory amendment occurs.

sources.name: Bar & Bench
sources.blurb: Class action arbitrability remains contested: Indian law does not permit representative/class arbitration without explicit statutory amendment, creating tension between consumer protection and dispute finality.

reg.title: India's AI companies have a data privacy problem and most don't know it yet
reg.impact: DPDPA 2023 and its Rules 2025 impose mandatory consent-before-processing requirements, explicit data use limitations, and localization obligations that directly conflict with many existing AI training and deployment practices; non-compliance triggers enforcement action by the Data Protection Board and potential penalties.
reg.action: AI companies should immediately audit their data processing pipelines for DPDPA compliance, establish consent management systems, map data localization requirements, and review third-party data licensing arrangements before Rules enforcement begins.

sources.name: Bar & Bench
sources.blurb: Indian AI companies face material compliance gaps under DPDPA 2023 and its Rules 2025, particularly around consent frameworks and data localization, creating liability exposure that most founders have not adequately assessed.

reg.title: Strengthening Negotiable Instruments: SC holds rebuttal of Section 139 must await trial
reg.impact: In cheque-bounce prosecutions under the Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, accused parties can no longer file preliminary applications to rebut the statutory presumption created by Section 139(2); all defences-including 'no consideration', 'conditional delivery', or 'post-dated cheque'-must be deferred to the substantive trial stage.
reg.action: Defence counsel should abandon pre-trial motions challenging Section 139 presumptions and consolidate defences for cross-examination and argument at trial; prosecutors can streamline dishonour proceedings by resisting interim rebuttal applications as premature.

sources.name: Bar & Bench
sources.blurb: SC's ruling that Section 139 rebuttal cannot succeed at the cheque-bounce stage clarifies that dishonour creates a presumption of debt that shifts burden to the accused-requiring full trial evidence rather than preliminary contestation.

reg.title: AI-assisted filings need a court-ready provenance record
reg.impact: Practice will shift to require: (1) mandatory AI disclosure in filings where AI was used; (2) documented review and modification logs; (3) explicit lawyer sign-off on AI-generated content with attestation of human verification; (4) potential liability exposure for filings lacking provenance records.
reg.action: Transactional lawyers should: (1) immediately audit AI usage in document drafting; (2) implement internal protocols documenting AI prompts, outputs, and human modifications; (3) create attestation templates for court filings disclosing AI assistance with provenance; (4) engage with bar councils (BCI) and court committees on emerging standards before they are mandated.

sources.name: Bar & Bench
sources.blurb: Indian courts and bar councils must establish mandatory provenance documentation standards for AI-assisted legal filings to ensure authenticity, lawyer accountability, and defensibility against challenges.

trends.summary: The absence of a formal Arbitration Council under the 1996 Act reflects India's implicit choice to leave arbitration governance to market players rather than statutory infrastructure. trends.title: Stop asking whether arbitration is dead, start asking why it isn't delivering
trends.summary: The article challenges the narrative of arbitration's decline in India, arguing instead that the real issue is systemic underperformance in speed, cost efficiency, and enforceability. Rather than questioning arbitration's viability, practitioners and policymakers should focus on identifying bottlenecks-excessive procedural steps, tribunal delays, and enforcement complications-that make arbitration functionally uncompetitive against litigation in many commercial disputes.

trends.title: A river became a deity and a person between two hearings: Tamirabarani and the turn to spiritual ecology

This jurisprudence treats rivers not as property or resource but as rights-bearing beings, forcing courts and administrators to balance spiritual/cultural significance with environmental protection and imposing affirmative duties on state and private actors.

trends.title: Brand protection in the era of social commerce

trends.title: When a breach has no remedy: No-claim, no-damage clauses
trends.summary: No-claim, no-damage clauses attempt to exclude liability for contractual breaches while preserving the substantive obligation itself, creating a paradox: performance is mandated but non-performance carries no legal consequence. Indian courts have increasingly scrutinized these clauses under principles of public policy and unconscionability, particularly where they insulate deliberate or gross breach from remedy.

trends.title: Confusing application of the Initial Interest Confusion doctrine in trade mark cases
trends.summary: The Initial Interest Confusion (IIC) doctrine-which protects against marks that deceive consumers at the point of initial attraction despite post-purchase clarification-has been unevenly applied across Indian trademark litigation. Courts have oscillated between adopting and rejecting the doctrine without clear jurisprudential guidelines, leaving practitioners uncertain about likelihood of confusion standards and the scope of trademark protection in digital and retail contexts.
